ecology.yield_intro: A shared stock (the commons, the forest) regrows a little every month. The most it can regrow in a month, at its best, is its maximum sustainable yield, and it regrows that much only when it is about half full. Taking more than it regrows shrinks the stock, which shrinks the regrowth, which makes the same harvest even further over the line.

markets.cost_plus_body: Firms set prices from their costs plus a markup. They do not raise a price when shelves empty. Empty shelves make a firm hire and produce more instead, so the quantity adjusts and the price does not. Wages and rents do respond to scarcity. A textbook market lets every price move with scarcity; this model is simpler on purpose, and each card says which rule it follows.
markets.cost_plus_title: How prices are set in this town
markets.empty: The markets appear once the first month has been played.
markets.intro_body: Every society has to decide what to make, how to make it and who gets it, when nobody knows everything. A market answers with prices: buyers and sellers adjust to what is scarce. It is one way of coordinating an economy, not the only one. This town uses several, and each card below says which ones it leans on.
markets.intro_not_capitalism: A market does not mean capitalism. Who owns the firms is a separate question.

systems.name: Market capitalism
systems.tagline: Owners keep the profits; wages follow the labour market.
systems.coordination: Leans on markets for prices, wages, homes and loans. The state sets taxes and rules around them.

facts.label: Wages
facts.value: Set by the market (a reserve army of unemployed holds them down)

systems.resistance: Not described in the design doc.

tradeoffs.label: Strength
tradeoffs.value: Fast growth driven by profit and investment (the growth loop in the design doc).

tradeoffs.label: Cost
tradeoffs.value: Growth also drives emissions up, and wealth can capture policy through lobbying.

systems.name: Regulated capitalism
systems.tagline: Owners still profit, but wages have a higher floor and lobbying is capped.
systems.coordination: Still market prices, but more rules: a higher wage floor, a cap on lobbying and room for community management of the commons.

facts.label: Wages
facts.value: Market wages with a higher floor

facts.label: Unlocks
facts.value: A campaign-spending cap and community management of the commons

tradeoffs.label: Strength
tradeoffs.value: Unlocks the campaign-spending cap and community management of the commons, and lowers the ceiling on lobbying. The emissions cap works in every system.

tradeoffs.label: Cost
tradeoffs.value: A long transition with some output lost while it lasts.

tradeoffs.label: Trade-off
tradeoffs.value: Lower GDP growth than market capitalism, in return for a better chance of staying inside the carbon budget (a design target, not a promise).

systems.name: Worker cooperatives
systems.tagline: Employees share the surplus and own the firms.
systems.coordination: Markets still price goods and jobs, but inside each firm the workers who own it decide together how to share the surplus, and the commons is managed by the community.

facts.label: Wages
facts.value: A share of surplus, with a floor

facts.label: Credit
facts.value: Banks distrust co-ops: a spread is added

systems.resistance: High resistance. The doc does not say from whom; expect owners and lenders.

tradeoffs.label: Strength
tradeoffs.value: Profits go to workers, which pulls inequality down, and lobbying power is lowest.

tradeoffs.label: Cost
tradeoffs.value: A long transition with some output lost while it lasts; workers need training.

tradeoffs.label: Trade-off
tradeoffs.value: Slower growth, and not a free pass on emissions.

mechanisms.label: Market
mechanisms.blurb: Buyers and sellers meet and prices signal what is scarce. Shops, jobs, homes and loans in this town work this way.
mechanisms.example: A shop, a job advert, a flat to rent.

mechanisms.label: Rules and planning
mechanisms.blurb: An authority sets quantities, prices or limits instead of letting prices decide: public housing rents, the minimum wage, the carbon price, the bank's capital rule, and the sharing-out of electricity when there is not enough.
mechanisms.example: Wartime rationing, public housing, the central plans of the Soviet system.

mechanisms.label: Firm (hierarchy)
mechanisms.blurb: Inside a firm, managers direct work instead of buying every step on a market. How many people a firm tries to hire is decided this way.
mechanisms.example: A factory manager deciding how many shifts to run (Ronald Coase).

mechanisms.label: Community rules
mechanisms.blurb: People share a resource under rules they set and enforce together, without prices or an owner. The town commons can work this way.
mechanisms.example: A village pasture, a co-operative (Elinor Ostrom).

columns.help: The loan the firm asked for, in dollars.

columns.label: Approved
columns.help: What the bank lent, in dollars. The bank lends less when the firm is already deep in debt or the bank is near its own limit.

columns.label: Rate
columns.help: The yearly cost of the loan, written as the dollars of interest a year for every $100 borrowed.

columns.label: Outcome
columns.help: Whether the request was approved in full, in part or refused.

columns.label: When
columns.help: Which month of the game this trade happened in. An older turn is summed over its three months.

list.label: Electricity
list.blurb: Firms and households use electricity. The power plants can produce only so much each month.
list.priceNote: Electricity has no price in this model. It is a quantity limit: if demand is higher than the plants can supply, everyone's use is cut back in the same proportion. The commons is the other resource with no price; see Ecology.

verdict.balanced: Firms and homes wanted {demand} {demand_unit} and the plants could supply {supply}: everyone was served in full.
verdict.short: Firms and homes wanted {demand} {demand_unit} but the plants could supply {supply}: {unmet} {unmet_unit} were not delivered, so output and comfort were cut back in proportion.
verdict.glut: Firms and homes wanted {demand} {demand_unit} and the plants could supply {supply}: {unsold} {unsold_unit} of capacity sat idle.
verdict.both: Firms and homes wanted {demand} {demand_unit}; {unmet} {unmet_unit} were not delivered while {unsold} {unsold_unit} sat idle.

trades.intro: Energy has no list of trades: the model has one town-wide supply and one town-wide demand, with no record of which household or firm used which plant's electricity.
trades.empty: Energy is counted for the whole town, not trade by trade.
